record.field: Escodoo - ERP for industry and manufacturing

div.p: You know what you sold. You are less sure what it cost you, when it will be ready, and whether the material is on the shelf. That gap is where the margin goes.
This page is for companies that transform material into product, with a bill of material and a shop floor.
Someone rebuilds the production plan every Monday from stock, orders and memory. When that person is on holiday, the factory improvises.
Purchasing buys against a forecast nobody trusts, so you carry stock you do not need and stop the line for a part that costs almost nothing.
The price list is based on last year plus a feeling. Scrap, rework and machine time are not in it, which means some of your best selling products lose money.
A customer complaint arrives and finding which batch, which supplier and which operator takes two days of somebody's week.

div.a: Talk it through in thirty minutes

div.h2: What you start being able to measure

div.p: On-time delivery against the promised date
Real cost per product against the standard
Scrap and rework rate per production line
Inventory turns and stock cover in days
Line stoppages caused by missing material
Lead time from order to shipment

t.t-value: 'From three disconnected systems to one operation'
'Production, stock and invoicing on the same records, with traceability from the customer order to the fiscal document, and a cost per product the commercial team can actually price against.'

div.p: We do not just deliver screens and forms. We structure operations.

record.field: Escodoo - ERP for trade and distribution

div.p: Your margin is thin and your working capital is sitting on a shelf. Everything depends on buying the right quantity and shipping without mistakes, which is exactly what nobody can see clearly.
This page is for companies that buy to resell, across one or several warehouses and channels.

div.h3: Stock says one thing, the shelf says another
div.p: Sales promises what is not there and refuses what is. Every count finds differences nobody can explain, because negative stock was allowed all along.
Fast movers run out, slow movers occupy the warehouse and the cash. Nobody has the coverage number in front of them when the decision is made.

div.h3: Picking depends on who is on shift
div.p: The experienced picker is fast and accurate. The new one is neither, and the cost of that shows up as a customer complaint two days later.

div.h3: Nobody knows the margin per order
div.p: Freight, discount, tax and payment terms all move it, and none of them are in the report the sales team looks at.

div.a: Talk it through in thirty minutes

div.h2: What you start being able to measure

div.p: Stock accuracy against the physical count
Order fill rate and stockout frequency
Picking errors per thousand lines
Inventory turns per product family
Margin per order, after freight and tax
Days from order received to dispatch

t.t-value: 'Picking that stopped depending on who was on shift'
'Multi warehouse replenishment, barcode-guided picking and a delivery promise the sales team can make without checking with the warehouse first.'

div.p: We do not just deliver screens and forms. We structure operations.
You sell your team's time and you are not sure where it went. Contracts renew late, hours are billed from memory, and the profitable clients are not necessarily the ones you think.
This page is for companies that sell hours, projects or contracts rather than equipment.

li.a: Your team travels to the client

div.h3: Hours are recorded after the fact
div.p: On Friday, from memory, into a spreadsheet. Whatever is billed from that is wrong in one direction or the other, and usually against you.
Nobody owns the renewal date, the price adjustment or the scope creep that happened during the year.
Message, e-mail, phone call, corridor. No queue, no priority, no record, and no way to show a client what you actually did for them.
You take on work without knowing whether the team can absorb it, then discover the answer during delivery.

div.a: Talk it through in thirty minutes

div.h2: What you start being able to measure

div.p: Billable share of the team's hours
Margin per client and per contract
Hours delivered against hours sold
Contract renewal and churn rate
Response time against what you promised
Revenue per employee

t.t-value: 'Every hour in the field turned into an invoice'
'Scheduling, worksheets with evidence and billing generated from the timesheet instead of reconstructed from a spreadsheet at the end of the month.'

div.p: We do not just deliver screens and forms. We structure operations.
Your revenue is produced by people you cannot see. The visit happened, probably. The part was used, apparently. The client will be invoiced, eventually.
This page is for companies whose teams travel to the client to execute the work.

li.a: You maintain assets on a plan

div.p: Somebody spends the morning calling technicians to find out where they are and whether they can take one more job.

div.h3: The van is an unaudited warehouse
div.p: Parts leave stock and reappear as a mystery. Some jobs fail because the part was in the wrong van.
A client disputes a visit and there is no signature, no photo and no arrival time to point at.

div.h3: Billing lags the work by weeks
div.p: Hours and parts are transcribed from paper at the end of the month, so the invoice is both late and smaller than it should be.

div.a: Talk it through in thirty minutes

div.h2: What you start being able to measure

div.p: First time fix rate
Visits per technician per day
Travel time as a share of paid time
Days from visit completed to invoice issued
Parts consumed against parts issued to vans
Response time against the agreed level

Maintenance is either planned or it is an emergency, and emergencies cost several times as much. Most teams know that and still spend their week reacting.
This page is for teams that maintain assets on a plan, whether the assets are yours or your client's.

li.a: Your team travels to the client
You maintain your own production line

div.h3: The plan exists on paper only
div.p: Preventive work is scheduled in a spreadsheet and skipped whenever something breaks, which is most weeks.
The same machine fails the same way every quarter and nobody notices, because each intervention is recorded separately or not at all.
Missing parts delay the work; excess parts trap capital in a store nobody has counted this year.
Contract renewal comes up and you have no report showing what you did, how fast you responded and what it prevented.

div.a: Talk it through in thirty minutes

div.h2: What you start being able to measure

div.p: Preventive against corrective work ratio
Mean time between failures per asset
Mean time to repair
Asset availability
Maintenance cost per asset per period
Plan adherence

Equipment comes in, sits on a bench, and the client calls to ask where it is. Somebody walks to the workshop to find out. That walk is your process.
This page is for operations where the equipment arrives at your bench, gets diagnosed and goes back.

li.a: Your team travels to the client
You maintain assets on a plan

div.h3: Nobody can say where an item is
div.p: Received, diagnosed, waiting for a part, waiting for approval, done. The status lives in a technician's head.

div.h3: Quotes wait for approval by phone
div.p: The repair stops until somebody reaches the client, and nobody is tracking how many days that costs you per month.
Whether this repair is covered depends on who is asked, which means you absorb costs you should not and charge for some you should not.
The same serial number comes back for the third time and it looks like a new job, because there is no history per unit.

div.a: Talk it through in thirty minutes

div.h2: What you start being able to measure

div.p: Turnaround time per repair type
Days lost waiting for client approval
Repeat repair rate per serial number
Warranty cost against billable repairs
Bench occupancy and work in progress
Margin per repair

The project is on schedule until the week it obviously is not. By then the hours are spent, the scope has moved twice and nobody wrote down who agreed to what.
This page is for companies that deliver work as projects, with a scope, a deadline and a budget.

li.a: You sell recurring hours and contracts
The process itself is the problem

div.p: Status comes from a meeting rather than from the work, so a project can be reported as eighty percent complete for two months.
You find out the project lost money when the accounting closes, which is far too late to do anything about it.
Small extras accumulate with no change record, and the argument about them happens at the end when the relationship is already strained.
Two project managers assign the same specialist to the same week, and neither finds out until it matters.

div.a: Talk it through in thirty minutes

div.h2: What you start being able to measure

div.p: Margin per project, while it is running
Hours consumed against hours planned
Deadline adherence per project type
Team utilisation and forecast capacity
Approved changes against unbilled extras
Days from milestone reached to invoice
We do not just deliver screens and forms. We structure operations.
